opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core problem we were stuck on for a long time is that when you look inside a neural network and try to understand what an individual neuron is doing, it usually isn't doing one thing. You'll find a neuron that fires on, say, references to academic citations, but also on Korean text, and also on some particular HTTP pattern. That's polysemanticity, and the leading explanation for it is superposition: the model has far more concepts it wants to represent than it has neurons, so it packs them in as overlapping directions in activation space. It's actually a pretty clever compression trick on the model's part, because most features are sparse. Any given input only activates a handful of them, so the interference between them stays manageable.

The problem is that this makes the neuron basis basically the wrong lens for interpretability. If you stare at neurons, you're looking at a tangle of many concepts projected onto each axis.

What sparse autoencoders do is give you a principled way to undo that compression. You train an autoencoder on the model's internal activations with a hidden layer that's much wider than the original layer, sometimes by a factor of tens or hundreds, and you put a sparsity penalty on it so that only a few latent units fire for any input. Because you're matching the assumption baked into superposition, that the true features are numerous but sparse, the autoencoder tends to recover directions that are far more monosemantic. Suddenly you get a feature that's just "DNA sequences," or "the Golden Gate Bridge," or "code that contains a security vulnerability," and you can verify that by looking at what activates it and what happens when you steer with it.

There are a few reasons I think that's a real step change and not just a nicer visualization.

First, it's unsupervised. You don't have to decide in advance which concepts you're looking for. Earlier methods like probing require you to bring a hypothesis and a labeled dataset. With SAEs the model tells you what its own vocabulary is, and a lot of what comes out is stuff nobody would have thought to probe for.

Second, it scales. The early results were on tiny toy models and one-layer transformers, and a lot of people reasonably wondered whether it would hold up on frontier-scale models. Then we saw it work on production-size models with millions of features, and the features stayed interpretable. That was the moment it went from an interesting research idea to something you could build on.

Third, and this is the part that matters most to me, the features are causal handles, not just correlates. You can clamp a feature up or down and the model's behavior changes in the way you'd predict. That turns interpretability from a descriptive science into something closer to an engineering discipline. You can start asking: can I find the feature responsible for this failure, and can I intervene on it directly instead of retraining or prompt-patching around it?

Now, I don't want to oversell it. SAEs have real limitations. The reconstruction isn't perfect, so there's some "dark matter" in the model you aren't explaining. Feature splitting means the granularity you get depends on dictionary size, so there isn't one canonical set of features. And features alone don't give you the full picture of computation; you need to understand how they interact across layers, which is where work on transcoders and circuit tracing comes in.

But as a foundation, it's the first time we've had a scalable, general method for decomposing a network into pieces that humans can actually read. That's why I think of it as the turning point. Before it, mechanistic interpretability was a lot of careful hand analysis of small circuits. After it, you can realistically imagine debugging and editing real models.

r002.rationale: It describes concepts as overlapping directions in activation space, but does not say those directions are near-orthogonal.

r003.rationale: It describes sparse autoencoders as an unsupervised way to undo representational compression and recover more monosemantic, interpretable features.

r004.rationale: It identifies scaling from toy models to production-size models with millions of features as a significant step for interpretability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the core problem sparse autoencoders attack is one that frustrated interpretability for years. When you look at a single neuron in a model, you'd hope it means one thing. In practice, it doesn't. It fires for a dozen unrelated concepts at once. We call that polysemanticity, and the leading explanation for it is superposition: the network wants to represent far more features than it has dimensions, so it packs them in at angles, overlapping, like a compressed code. The model can get away with this because most features are rarely active at the same time, so the interference is tolerable.

That's a beautiful theory, but for a long time it was mostly theory, backed by toy models. What made SAEs significant is that they gave us a practical way to actually undo the compression. You take the activations, project them into a much wider space, and train with a sparsity penalty so that only a handful of directions are active for any given input. When you do that, the features that pop out are, surprisingly often, clean and human-interpretable. One direction fires on legal citations, another on a specific programming idiom, another on a particular emotional tone. Things no individual neuron would have shown you.

I'd point to three reasons that matters. First, it's scalable and unsupervised. You're not hand-picking concepts to probe for. You hand the model's own activations to the method and it tells you what the model is representing, including things you'd never have thought to look for. Second, it turned superposition from a hypothesis into something we can measure. You can see how many features live in a layer, how they're distributed, how they split as you make the dictionary bigger. Third, and this is the part that excites me most, the features are causal handles. You can turn one up or down and watch the model's behavior change in a way that matches the interpretation. That moves interpretability from description toward intervention.

I don't want to oversell it. SAEs have real limitations. There's reconstruction error, features can split or merge depending on dictionary size, and some of what they find is clearly an artifact of the method rather than something the model "believes." But as a first tool that actually gets a grip on the superposition problem at scale, in real frontier models, I think they're a genuine step change.

r002.rationale: It describes features packed at angles and overlapping, but does not characterize them as near-orthogonal directions.

r003.rationale: It explains that SAEs use a sparsity penalty to surface clean, human-interpretable features from activations without hand-picked concepts.

r004.rationale: It calls SAEs scalable and says they provide a grip on superposition at scale in real frontier models.

astra-6.text:
The key idea behind superposition is that a network can represent more features than it has dimensions. So an individual neuron might participate in several different concepts, and looking at that neuron alone doesn’t tell you what the network is doing.

Sparse autoencoders give us a practical way to try to disentangle those representations. You take the network’s activations and learn a larger set of features that can reconstruct them, with the constraint that only a small number of features are active for any particular input. That encourages the autoencoder to find recurring pieces of the representation that would otherwise be mixed together.

What makes that exciting is that it turns superposition from an explanation for why networks are hard to interpret into something we can investigate experimentally. We can inspect the recovered features, see what activates them, and test whether changing them affects the model’s behavior.

There’s still a gap between finding a feature that looks interpretable and establishing that we’ve understood the computation. The decomposition isn’t guaranteed to be complete or uniquely correct. But it gives us a much more useful unit of analysis than individual neurons, and that’s a substantial step forward.

r001.rationale: It says networks can represent more features than they have dimensions, but does not connect this pressure to internet-scale information or a limited parameter budget.

r002.rationale: It describes mixed representations but does not explain that concepts are represented along near-orthogonal directions in latent space.

r003.rationale: It explains that sparse autoencoders learn sparse feature representations from activations, disentangle mixed concepts, and yield features that can be inspected.

r004.rationale: It presents sparse autoencoders as useful for experimental investigation but does not address scalability to large neural networks.

sol-6.1.text:
The core difficulty with superposition is that a model can represent more features than it has neurons. So if you inspect individual neurons, you often see a mixture of concepts, and it’s hard to tell what the model is actually representing.

Sparse autoencoders give us a way to disentangle that mixture. We train them to reconstruct the model’s activations using a larger set of candidate features, with the constraint that only a few should be active for any given input. That lets us look for meaningful directions in activation space rather than assuming each neuron corresponds to one concept.

What makes that significant is that it turns superposition from an explanation for why networks are difficult to interpret into something we can investigate empirically. We can identify candidate features, examine when they activate, and test what happens when we intervene on them. It’s not a complete solution—the features aren’t guaranteed to be faithful or interpretable—but it gives us a much better experimental handle on the problem.

r001.rationale: It says models can represent more features than neurons, but does not explain this as pressure from compressing internet-scale information into a limited parameter budget.

r002.rationale: It describes features as directions in activation space, but does not characterize them as near-orthogonal directions.

r003.rationale: It describes sparse autoencoders disentangling activation mixtures into candidate features, but does not clearly identify this as unsupervised interpretation into concepts; it also cautions that features are not guaranteed to be interpretable.

r004.rationale: It presents sparse autoencoders as a useful experimental handle, but does not discuss their scalability to large neural networks.
